claims.text: Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 is a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy considered for amorphous-phase formation.
Melt-spinning provides cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s for this alloy.
Very rapid cooling by melt-spinning produces an amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 structure.
Phosphorus addition enhances the glass-forming ability of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 during rapid cooling.
An ultra-rapid quench followed by a sub-Tg hold promotes controlled structural relaxation.
The sub-Tg hold reduces free volume.
The sub-Tg hold enhances short- to medium-range atomic ordering.
Annealing at about Tg - 5 K can leave an amorphous structure stable without initiating crystallization.
The proposed sub-Tg hold relieves internal stress.
The proposed hold converts or relaxes a high-energy as-quenched glass toward a lower-energy glass state.
The relaxed lower-energy amorphous state has improved thermal stability.
The two-stage treatment delays subsequent crystallization upon heating relative to continuous ultra-rapid quenching.
The two-stage treatment increases the amorphous phase fraction relative to a single-stage ultra-rapid quench.
A post-quench sub-Tg hold improves glass-forming ability relative to single-stage ultra-rapid quenching.
A hold too far below Tg will not produce the predicted improvement.
A hold too close to crystallization or of excessive duration can produce partial crystallization.
The treatment may fail in alloy systems where phosphorus does not sufficiently suppress crystalline nucleation.
Phosphorus addition may entail reduced ductility or related mechanical-property limitations.

contradictions.description: The intervention places the sub-Tg hold after the initial quench and describes it as noncrystallizing relaxation of an already formed amorphous state, yet the predicted outcome says that this post-solidification hold increases glass-forming ability and amorphous fraction. The stated mechanism explains stabilization of an existing glass but not how the later hold changes whether glass formed during the preceding quench.
